text:
Google DeepMind built a tool that interrogates an image instead of judging it.

What changed: Backstory is in limited testing through Google's Trusted Testers program with journalists, fact-checkers, OSINT researchers and librarians.

What it actually does: you give it one image. It runs a chain of checks using Gemini and a set of agents, deciding which tool fits each step. Is this AI-generated. Has it been manipulated. Where has it appeared before. What was the surrounding context each time. Then it returns a readable report with citations and the steps it took to get there.

Why builders should care: provenance just became a workflow instead of a gut feeling. And if you publish AI-assisted work, that same trail exists for yours.

Try this this week: before you repost an image, run by hand the three checks Backstory automates. Reverse-search it. Find the earliest appearance. Read the caption that originally sat under it. Then go label your own AI-generated work properly.

The bigger signal: the argument is moving from "is it real" to "can you show your sources." That is a workflow question, and workflow questions are the ones builders get to answer.

Save this for your AI stack.

text:
Most people are debugging the wrong thing.

When AI hands back generic output, the instinct is to rewrite the prompt. Ten versions later it is still generic, because the prompt was never the problem. The model has nothing to work from.

We proved it on Tech Thursday. A client's whole brand voice came back from one plain request. Tone, copy rules, hero page, call to action. It worked because everything it needed was already in the folder.

Five things to hand it before you ask for anything:

1. The raw files. Documents, exports, notes, the actual material.
2. The voice. Past work that already sounds right.
3. The constraints. What it must never say or do.
4. One finished example. The bar, made concrete.
5. The audience. Who this is actually for.

Do that and the prompt becomes one sentence.
